info.name: Dynamic Alarm: Backend
info.description:
Everything the app never calls.

Two kinds of thing live here. The health check is served by our API but read by uptime monitors and load balancers rather than by the phone. The rest are the upstream NS and TomTom calls the backend makes on the app's behalf, reproduced exactly as the server sends them.

Those upstream requests are the reason this collection exists. When a wake time comes back wrong, the question is almost always whether the API composed the journey badly or whether NS answered oddly, and the only way to separate the two is to make the same call by hand. Every diagnosis in this project so far has come from doing that: the subscription refusing door-to-door planning, and `stations/nearest` returning a railway museum with no scheduled service.

**These requests spend the shared NS budget.** 300 requests per 5 minutes for the whole deployment, not per user. Do not point a Postman Runner at the NS folder.

The simulation requests are the exception to "everything the app never calls": the app's debug panel uses them too. They live here because they are a test tool rather than part of the product, and because using them by hand is the point.

`deviceToken` is a real device's bearer token, and `occurrenceId` one of its armed mornings. Both come from the app collection's register and occurrences requests.

The keys go in a Postman environment, never in this file. `apps/api/.env` holds the real ones.

item.name: 1. Operations

request.description:
The one response deliberately outside the `{ success, data }` envelope, because load balancers and uptime checks do not know about it. The status code carries the same answer, so nothing is lost.

200 when the database is reachable, 503 when it is not. The database is reported as its own field rather than folded into one boolean: a process that is up but cannot reach MySQL is exactly the state where the monitor loop silently stops moving alarms, and "ok" would hide it.

Response: `HealthResponse`.

One pass of the monitor loop. On the VPS the Ofelia scheduler calls this once a minute by running `node dist/tools/monitorTick.js` inside the container; this request is the same call by hand.

Each call also sweeps the NS disruptions feed **once for every user**, a flat 1440 requests a day whatever the number of alarms, and pulls any occurrence travelling through an affected station forward to be checked immediately. Beyond that it claims only the occurrences whose `nextCheckAt` has arrived, so most calls do nothing at all and answer `claimed: 0`. That is the normal night, not a fault. Each claimed occurrence costs one NS or TomTom request, so running this in a Postman Runner spends the shared quota as fast as it can.

Authenticated with `X-Monitor-Token`, not a device token: the tick belongs to no device, and handing the scheduler a phone's credential would let a stolen token drive the loop for everyone. An unset `MONITOR_TOKEN` on the server answers 503 rather than running unguarded.

Safe to call twice: claiming uses `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` with a five minute lease, and a tick that overlaps a running one answers `skipped: true` and does nothing.

Response: `MonitorTickResponse`.

**Test only, and it invents nothing but the timetable.** The monitor applies this on its next check of that occurrence; everything after that is the real path, the same engine recomputing, the same opt-in settings deciding whether the alarm may move, the same push through Expo, and the same monotonic rule on the phone.

Device authenticated, and it can only touch that device's own morning: a simulation aimed at somebody else's alarm is a way to make a stranger late.

Staging one sets `nextCheckAt` to now, so the next tick picks it up rather than the next cadence band. Locally nothing ticks on its own, so run the **Monitor tick** request above, or `npm run tick -w @alarm/api`.

It expires after an hour, and is consumed by the check that applies it, so it cannot be applied twice. The occurrence reports `simulated`, and the alarm event written for the change is prefixed `SIMULATED:`, because someone woken early by a test must be able to tell that from the product being wrong.

Shifts the stored journey later by `minutes` and marks it disrupted, so the risk buffer responds the way it would to a real delay rather than only the arithmetic being exercised. Every leg moves, not just the first: a train that leaves late arrives late, and shifting one end would invent a journey that gains time in transit.

The alarm only actually moves if the device has **sleep longer on delays** switched on. A run where nothing moves and the setting is off is the setting working, not a failed test.

`minutes` is capped at 180. Four hours of pretend delay makes the journey infeasible, which is a different test with a different name.

item.description: Served by our API, not called by the app.

item.name: 2. NS Reisinformatie (upstream)
Trips, station to station, arriving by

request.description:
The rail half of every journey.

Station to station only. Passing coordinates instead returns `API_KEY_NOT_ALLOWED_TO_PLAN_DOOR_TO_DOOR` on this subscription, which is why `JourneyPlannerService` composes door to door from this plus TomTom walking legs.

`addChangeTime` goes to the planner rather than being applied afterwards, so a connection tighter than the user's transfer buffer is never proposed. Padding the result could not achieve that, because it cannot change which train was chosen.

`searchForArrival` has no lower bound, and that is worth knowing: for a station with sparse service it will happily answer with the last train that ever got there, possibly the previous evening. Such a trip satisfies the deadline arithmetic and produces a wake time in the past, so the planner drops departures already gone.

The mechanism that makes the product honest.

Rather than adding a reported delay to a stored plan, NS reconstructs the same itinerary and says what it now looks like, including whether the connection still works. Copy a `ctxRecon` from the trips response above into the collection variable.

When it can no longer be reconstructed the answer means "plan again", never "no change".

How an address becomes a departure station.

**Read `heeftVertrektijden` on every result.** These exact coordinates return Utrecht Maliebaan first, 755 metres away, which is the railway museum and has no scheduled service. Planning from it produced a journey eight hours adrift that passed every internal check. The API over-fetches and filters on that field for this reason, and there is no way to ask the server to do it.

The answer is stable for a given home or office, so it is cached rather than re-asked per plan.

What the app's `/places/autosuggest` proxies.

**The `type` filter is not a refinement, it is required.** Without it the response contains addresses only, so a user typing "Utrecht Centraal" is offered four streets and no station. Drop the parameter and compare.

Results come back grouped by type, each group holding a `locations` array. The API flattens that.

Swept once globally per monitor tick in M2, not once per user.

A flat 1440 calls a day regardless of how many people use the app. Anything touching a station an armed occurrence passes through promotes that occurrence to an immediate re-check, which catches a cancellation within about a minute even for someone sitting in the 30-minute polling band. No per-user cadence could afford that.

item.description:
What `NsModule` sends. Auth is the `Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key` header from the `Ns-App` product.

These share one ceiling of 300 requests per 5 minutes across the whole deployment, so use them one at a time.

item.name: 3. TomTom Routing (upstream)

request.description:
Car journeys, planned backwards from the arrival time.

**For a future `arriveAt`, live traffic is ignored.** Only historic and predictive data shape the road speeds, so a route calculated the night before is a forecast, and one calculated inside the departure window reflects the road as it is. The engine relaxes the risk buffer accordingly and the monitor re-queries as departure approaches. Comparing this request against the same one without `arriveAt` shows the difference directly.

Read `summary.travelTimeInSeconds` and `summary.trafficDelayInSeconds`. The second is congestion cost against free flow, which is what the app shows as a delay even though a road has no timetable.

The access legs that NS will not supply on this subscription.

A routed pedestrian time along real paths, which is a better number than a straight-line estimate and arguably better than what NS would have returned. Rounded up to whole minutes by the API, because the error that costs a train is being half a minute short, not half a minute early.

`traffic=false` is required: pedestrian routing rejects traffic-aware options, and a footpath has no congestion to model.

The same leg, cycled, which for most Dutch commuters is the real one.

Compare it against the pedestrian request above on the same coordinates. On a one-kilometre hop it is roughly twelve minutes on foot against three by bike; on a two-kilometre access leg the gap is around twenty minutes, applied straight to the wake-up time.

This is what `AccessMode.BIKE` selects. Until it existed, every access leg was computed as walking, silently, which was wrong at the home end for anyone who cycles and wrong in the direction that wakes them earlier than they need.

What `TomTomModule` sends. Auth is the `key` query parameter.

Separate quota from NS, and not the one that binds.
